data.summary: Who can read and change which source is controlled and auditable.
AI assistants work from the organisation's own examples, standards and checks.

eurekas.statement: A device refuses to install an unsigned package.

data.summary: Released artifacts are cryptographically signed and verified before use.
A new board build is qualified by an automated test run, not a manual campaign.

eurekas.statement: A release report links each requirement to its passing tests automatically.

data.summary: Requirement-to-test-to-release traces are generated, not hand-maintained.
New boards are brought up with a written, repeatable procedure.
unlocks: Second and third boards come up in days, not weeks

eurekas.statement: A broken commit is caught by CI before review.

data.summary: Every change is built and tested automatically before it merges.
The full development toolchain starts from one container definition.

data.benefit: Engineers find, reuse and build on what exists instead of rebuilding it.
data.summary: One front door to SDKs, APIs, examples, pipelines and their owners.
Every device has a hardware-rooted identity it can prove.

data.benefit: Changes are proven against a twin of the fielded system before they reach a single device.
data.summary: A live, faithful model of the deployed system that runs the real software.

nodes.description: Simulation + hardware abstraction + recorded I/O, from the write-up.
nodes.title: Digital Twin

data.summary: Working examples of how things are done are searchable in one place.
Deployed devices report health so problems are seen before users report them.

eurekas.statement: One production service uses a generated client.

data.summary: Interface clients are generated from the interface definitions.

eurekas.statement: One driver runs unchanged on two different boards.

data.summary: Applications use stable device interfaces instead of board-specific code.
Most development and testing happens without access to target hardware.
unlocks: Hardware stops being the schedule bottleneck

nodes.description: Simulation or recorded-data replay — either one, on top of the abstraction layer and SDK.

eurekas.statement: The platform image boots against simulated peripherals.

data.summary: The software runs against simulated peripherals and boards.

data.benefit: Every team tests against every supported board, continuously, without owning the boards.
data.summary: A shared lab of simulated and real hardware, booked and driven by automation.
Tests can drive and observe real hardware through a scripted harness.
Hardware-in-the-loop tests run automatically on every release candidate.
Every external interface has a written, versioned description.
unlocks: Teams integrate against a document instead of a person

data.benefit: Any engineering question — why, where, who, proven how — is answered in minutes.
data.summary: Requirements, designs, code, tests, examples and people are connected and queryable.
Engineers watch live system telemetry while testing.
Platform services are reached through one documented, versioned API.

eurekas.statement: A team outside the platform group ships an application using only the SDK.

data.summary: Teams build products on the platform from an SDK, without platform-team help.
unlocks: Product teams that start from the platform, not from scratch

data.summary: Fleet data predicts failures and schedules updates or service before they happen.
A release is one button press: build, test, sign, package, publish.
unlocks: Releases on demand instead of release weekends

eurekas.statement: A field bug is reproduced on a desk by replaying recorded traffic.

Releases follow a written checklist that produces the same result each time.

eurekas.statement: Two clean builds of the same commit produce identical images.

Software is delivered as versioned packages with declared dependencies.

tree.description:
DEMO / FICTIONAL. A Civilization-style capability tech tree for an embedded
Linux engineering platform: six eras (columns) by eight branches (swimlanes),
with capabilities, milestones and wonders joined by prerequisites. Capability
names and structure come from Eric's write-up; owners, links, eurekas and the
statuses in demo.state.json are invented for demonstration and describe no
real organisation. Links are opaque `{type, ref, relation}` references that a
host application resolves (e.g. against its example catalog).
tree.title: Engineering Platform
